title: The Binding of Isaac: God Will Provide
summary: God tests Abraham by commanding him to offer Isaac, his only son whom he loves, as a burnt offering on a mountain in the land of Moriah. Abraham obeys, binds Isaac on the altar, and raises the knife, but the angel of the LORD stops him, and Abraham sacrifices a ram caught in a thicket in his son's place. God swears by himself to bless Abraham and bless all nations through his offspring, and the chapter closes with news of Nahor's family, including Rebekah.
story:
Everything in Abraham's story has pointed toward Isaac. The promises of a nation, of descendants like the stars, and of blessing for all peoples all run through this one boy, born when Abraham was a hundred and Sarah ninety, after twenty-five years of waiting. In the chapter just before, Ishmael was sent away (21:14), and God told Abraham that ‘through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned’ (21:12). Now God asks for Isaac.

The chapter is the climax of Abraham's life of faith. His story began with a command to ‘go’ to a land God would show him (12:1), which cut him off from his past; it reaches its summit with the same command, to go to a mountain God will show him, which seems to cut him off from his future. It is the last time God speaks to Abraham in Genesis, and his final words are a sworn oath that gathers all the earlier promises. After this, the story turns toward the next generation. Sarah's death follows in chapter 23, and the list of Nahor's children at the end of this chapter quietly introduces Rebekah, who will become Isaac's wife in Genesis 24.
historical:
The land of Moriah is not otherwise identified in Genesis. Second Chronicles 3:1 says that Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem “on Mount Moriah”, where the LORD had appeared to David, and Jewish and Christian tradition has long identified Abraham's mountain with the temple mount. Jubilees 18:13 (second century BC) calls it Mount Zion, and Josephus says it was the mountain on which David later built the temple (Antiquities 1.226). The Samaritans, whose Pentateuch reads Moreh in verse 2, placed the event at Mount Gerizim near Shechem. Abraham was living at Beersheba (21:33, 22:19), about seventy kilometers (some forty-five miles) from Jerusalem in a straight line and farther by road, a distance that fits a trip of three days with a loaded donkey.

Child sacrifice was a real practice in parts of the ancient world. Second Kings 3:27 records that the king of Moab, Mesha (known from his own ninth-century inscription, the Mesha Stele), offered his firstborn son as a burnt offering on the city wall during a siege. Infant burials in the sanctuary called the tophet at Phoenician Carthage have long been debated: Jeffrey Schwartz and colleagues (PLoS ONE, 2010) argued that the remains show a cemetery of children who died near birth, while Patricia Smith and colleagues (Antiquity, 2011) and Paolo Xella and colleagues (2013) argued that they attest sacrifice. Within Israel, the kings Ahaz and Manasseh are said to have made their sons ‘pass through the fire’ (2 Kings 16:3, 21:6). Israel's law forbade the practice absolutely (Leviticus 18:21, 20:2-5; Deuteronomy 12:31), and the prophets condemned it as something God never asked: “something I never commanded, nor did it even enter My mind” (Jeremiah 7:31). Micah 6:7 lists offering one's firstborn as the extreme of misguided religion.

Genesis doesn't give Isaac's age. He is called na'ar (verses 5 and 12), a word used for a young child but also for Joseph at seventeen (37:2) and for young men of fighting age, and he is old enough to carry the wood for the fire up a mountain. Later tradition filled the gap. Josephus made him twenty-five (Antiquities 1.227). Genesis Rabbah 56:8 made him thirty-seven, with a variant reading of twenty-six, reasoning that a grown man could not be bound without his consent; the figure thirty-seven comes from Sarah's age, ninety at Isaac's birth and 127 at her death in the next chapter, on the traditional assumption, followed by Rashi, that she died on hearing of the binding.
cultural:
A burnt offering (olah, ‘that which goes up’) was a sacrifice wholly consumed by fire on the altar, given entirely to God; the worshiper kept nothing of it (Leviticus 1). Abraham carries what the ritual requires: fire, probably live coals in a vessel, a knife, and wood, and he builds an altar on the spot, arranges the wood, and places the victim on top, the same sequence Leviticus 1:7-8 prescribes. The ram caught by its horns, offered “in place of his son” (verse 13), introduces the idea of a substitute that will run through Israel's sacrificial system.

Firstborn sons held a special place in the ancient Near East as heirs and bearers of the family's future. Israel's law claimed every firstborn as belonging to God, but required that firstborn sons be redeemed rather than sacrificed: “every firstborn of your sons you must redeem” (Exodus 13:13, 34:20). Jon Levenson (The Death and Resurrection of the Beloved Son, 1993) argued that this law and the Akedah belong together: the claim of God on the beloved son is real, and it is met by substitution and redemption rather than death.

In Jewish tradition the chapter is called the Akedah, the binding, from the verb in verse 9. It is the Torah reading on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year (Genesis 21 is read on the first; many Reform congregations read chapter 22 on their single day). The ram's horn, the shofar, sounded on that day, is tied to the ram of verse 13 in the Babylonian Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 16a), where Rabbi Abbahu explains that God said to sound a ram's horn before him so that he would remember the binding of Isaac and count it as if Israel had bound themselves before him. The remembrance section (Zikhronot) of the additional (Musaf) service of Rosh Hashanah asks God to remember the binding in mercy for Isaac's descendants, recalling how Abraham suppressed his compassion to do God's will. Many prayer books place the chapter among the morning blessings for daily reading, followed by a prayer that as Abraham conquered his compassion for his son, so God's compassion would conquer his anger; Sephardi and Hasidic communities read it daily, and it is optional in Ashkenazi use. Behind these prayers stands the idea of zekhut avot, the merit of the fathers, in which the faithfulness of Abraham and Isaac is remembered in favor of their descendants.

Muslims commemorate Abraham's offering of his son, told in the Qur'an (37:99-111), at Eid al-Adha, the Feast of Sacrifice, when animals are sacrificed at the end of the pilgrimage season and their meat shared with family and the poor. The Qur'an does not name the son, and most Muslim commentators hold that he was Ishmael (see the second hard question).
literary:
This is one of the most tightly written narratives in the Bible. The narrator tells the reader at once that it is a test, but Abraham doesn't know that, and the text refuses to show his feelings. Erich Auerbach made this chapter the center of the opening essay, ‘Odysseus' Scar’, of his study of Western literature, Mimesis (1946). He contrasted Homer, who sets everything in the foreground, fully lit and fully explained, with Genesis 22, where only what matters for the action is expressed and everything else, time, place, thought, and feeling, is left in the dark, so that the story is ‘fraught with background’ and demands interpretation. The three days of silent travel, the unexplained command, and the unspoken thoughts of father and son are the heart of its power.

The command piles up its weight in stages: “Take your son,” then “your only son Isaac, whom you love”, and only at the end his name. The phrase for go in verse 2 (lekh-lekha) is the same unusual phrase used in Genesis 12:1, and “which I will show you” repeats that call too. Abraham's answer, “Here I am” (hinneni), comes three times, to God (verse 1), to Isaac (verse 7), and to the angel (verse 11), and it frames his availability to each. The line “the two of them walked on together” (verses 6 and 8) frames the only recorded conversation between Abraham and Isaac, and ‘together’ returns in verse 19. The chapter turns on the verb to see (raah): Abraham ‘lifts up his eyes and sees’ the place (verse 4) and the ram (verse 13), tells Isaac that God will ‘see to’ (provide) the lamb (verse 8), and names the place The LORD Will See or Provide (verse 14). The word place (maqom) recurs four times, anticipating the place God will choose for his name (Deuteronomy 12:5).

The chapter uses the name God (Elohim) in verses 1 to 10 and the LORD (YHWH) from the angel's call on, a shift that source critics have used to assign the core story to the Elohist and the second angelic speech to a later hand. R. W. L. Moberly (Vetus Testamentum 38, 1988) described verses 15 to 18 as ‘the earliest commentary on the Akedah’, a reflection within the text that interprets Abraham's obedience as the ground of the renewed promise. Read as it stands, the second speech is the climax: for the only time in Genesis God swears by himself, and the formula ‘declares the LORD’, common in the prophets, appears here alone in Genesis. The closing genealogy gives Nahor twelve sons, like Ishmael and later Jacob, and ends with the name that matters, Rebekah.

outline.t: Three days to the mountain; “God Himself will provide”
Isaac bound, the angel intervenes, a ram in his place
God swears by himself to bless Abraham
News of Nahor's family and the birth of Rebekah

doctrines.note: Abraham's faith is tested at the point where God's command seems to contradict God's promise, which ran through Isaac. He tells his servants “then we will return to you” (verse 5) and tells Isaac that God will provide the lamb (verse 8). Faith here trusts the Promiser more than the promised gift, and James 2:21-23 sees in this obedience the completion of the faith counted as righteousness in 15:6.

The ram dies “in place of his son” (verse 13). The chapter states the principle of substitution in its simplest form, one life given instead of another, and God himself provides the offering. The sacrificial system will develop the principle, and the New Testament applies it to Christ's death, the Lamb God provides.

The test ends with a verdict: “now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your only son from me” (verse 12). The fear of God is defined by what a person will not withhold from him. It is reverent trust shown in action, not terror, and it answers Abraham's own complaint in 20:11 that there was no fear of God in Gerar.

Genesis does not say how Abraham expected to return with Isaac, but Hebrews 11:19 draws out the logic of verse 5: “Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead, and in a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death.” The chapter becomes a pattern of a son given up and received back, which the New Testament fulfills in the resurrection of Jesus.

God confirms his promises with an oath: “By Myself I have sworn” (verse 16), since there is no one greater to swear by (Hebrews 6:13). The promise that all nations will be blessed through Abraham's offspring (verse 18) is restated as the covenant's goal, and these are God's last words to Abraham.

words.note: Nasah, to test or prove (about 36 occurrences). Standard lexicons describe it as putting someone to the proof to find out what is in them. God tests Israel in the wilderness ‘to know what was in your heart’ (Deuteronomy 8:2), and Israel is forbidden to test God (Deuteronomy 6:16). The test isn't God discovering something he didn't know, but bringing Abraham's trust into the open, as the angel's “now I know that you fear God” expresses in human terms. The King James Version's ‘tempt’ meant ‘try’ in 1611; James 1:13 says God tempts no one to evil.

Yachid, only, one and only (twelve occurrences). It is used of an only child mourned (Jeremiah 6:26, Amos 8:10, Zechariah 12:10) and of Jephthah's only daughter (Judges 11:34). Isaac was not Abraham's only child, since Ishmael lived, but he was the only son of the promise and the only son left in Abraham's house, the unique and irreplaceable heir. The word is repeated in verses 2, 12, and 16. The Septuagint rendered it agapētos, beloved, and Hebrews 11:17 calls Isaac Abraham's monogenēs, the word John uses of Jesus in John 3:16.

Ahav, to love (a little over 200 occurrences). Verse 2 is its first appearance in the Bible, and it describes a father's love for his son, spoken in the command to give that son up. The verb covers human love of every kind, God's love for Israel (Deuteronomy 7:8), and Israel's love for God (Deuteronomy 6:5). Placing its first use here makes the cost of the command explicit: God names the love before he asks for the son.

Olah, burnt offering (about 285 occurrences, most of them in Leviticus, Numbers, and the books of Chronicles). The name comes from the verb alah, to go up, and describes an offering that ascends entirely in smoke. The word appears six times in this chapter. It was Israel's most basic sacrifice, offered morning and evening (Exodus 29:38-42), and the olah of a ram in place of a son sets the pattern of substitution that the burnt offering carries through the law (Leviticus 1:4).

Aqad, to bind. This is its only occurrence in the Old Testament; a related adjective describes striped or banded animals in Genesis 30:35. Jewish tradition named the whole chapter from it, the Akedah, the binding. The rarity of the word draws attention to the act: the narrative that refuses to describe feelings pauses on the binding of the son, the moment that later Jewish tradition made central to its reading of Isaac's consent.

Raah, to see (about 1,300 occurrences, one of the commonest verbs in the Bible), here in the name Abraham gives the place, YHWH Yireh, The LORD Will Provide. To see to something is to provide it. Abraham had said God would see to the lamb (verse 8), and God did. The saying that follows uses the passive of the same verb, which can mean ‘it will be provided’ or ‘he will be seen’; the place where God sees to his people's need is the place where he is seen, the temple mountain of 2 Chronicles 3:1.

Tachat, under, below, and by extension instead of or in place of (about 500 occurrences in all its senses). In verse 13 the ram is offered tachat beno, “in place of his son”, the Bible's first plain statement of substitution in sacrifice. The same preposition describes one person or thing taking another's place, as when Seth is given ‘in place of Abel’ (Genesis 4:25).

Shava, to swear an oath (about 185 occurrences). It is related to the number seven, perhaps from oaths sealed by seven items, as at Beersheba, ‘well of the oath’ or ‘well of seven’ (21:28-31). In verse 16 God swears by himself, the first divine oath in Genesis, and later Scripture remembers this oath again and again as the oath sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Genesis 26:3, Exodus 32:13, Deuteronomy 1:8, Luke 1:73).

christ:
Christians have read this chapter in the light of the cross from the beginning. Paul's words in Romans 8:32, “He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all”, echo the Greek translation of Genesis 22:12 and 16, where Abraham did not spare his beloved son. The Greek of verse 2 calls Isaac Abraham's ‘beloved son’, and many hear that phrase behind the voice at Jesus' baptism: “You are My beloved Son” (Mark 1:11). John 3:16 says that God ‘gave His one and only Son’, and Hebrews 11:17 uses the same word, monogenēs, of Isaac. Hebrews 11:17-19 says Abraham, “when he was tested, offered up Isaac on the altar”, reasoning that God could raise the dead, and received him back ‘in a sense’, literally ‘as a figure’ (en parabolē), a word that invites reading the event as a pattern of resurrection. James 2:21-23 makes the same event the completion of Abraham's faith.

The early Christian writers traced the pattern further: a beloved son carrying the wood up a hill, as Jesus carried his cross (John 19:17); a place of sacrifice associated with Jerusalem; a trip of three days; and a lamb provided by God, which John the Baptist names when he calls Jesus “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). Some of these links are drawn by the New Testament (the beloved son, the only son, the resurrection figure); others, such as the wood and the cross, were drawn by later writers, and teachers should say which is which.

The great difference is also the point. Isaac was spared at the last moment, and a substitute died in his place; God did not spare his own Son. Isaac was a passive participant in Genesis (later Jewish tradition made him a willing one); Jesus gave himself (John 10:18). Abraham was told to stop; the Father went through with what he asked of no human father. Finally, the oath of verse 18, that through Abraham's offspring all nations will be blessed, is read by Paul as the gospel announced in advance (Galatians 3:8) and by Peter as fulfilled in the Servant God raised up (Acts 3:25-26). Jon Levenson, writing as a Jewish scholar, argued that the story of the beloved son given up and restored is the shared root from which both the Jewish memory of the Akedah and the Christian proclamation of the cross grew, a claim that lets Christians see how deep the chapter's pattern runs in Israel's Scripture.
interpretation:
No chapter of Genesis has a richer history of reading. Second Temple writers already expanded it. Jubilees 17:15-18:19 has Prince Mastema challenge Abraham's loyalty before God, as Satan does in Job, and a Qumran text (4Q225) does the same. Pseudo-Philo's Biblical Antiquities 32 gives Isaac a speech of willing consent, and 4 Maccabees (13:12, 16:20) holds him up as a model for martyrs. Philo (On Abraham 167-207) defends Abraham against critics who compared him to pagans who sacrificed children. The Targums Neofiti and Pseudo-Jonathan have Isaac ask to be bound well so that he will not flinch and spoil the offering, and Genesis Rabbah 55-56 and the Talmud (Sanhedrin 89b) add Satan's accusations and the dialogue in which each phrase of verse 2 answers Abraham's hesitation. Medieval Jewish poems written after the massacres of the Crusades, such as Ephraim of Bonn's in the twelfth century, even imagined Isaac slain and revived; Shalom Spiegel traced these legends in The Last Trial (Hebrew 1950, English 1967). Ibn Ezra rejected the idea that Isaac died as contrary to the text, and Maimonides (Guide of the Perplexed 3.24) found in the story the limit of the love and fear of God and the certainty prophets had in what they received.

The church fathers read the chapter typologically from the start. The Epistle of Barnabas (7:3) speaks of the type established in Isaac offered on the altar. Fragments of Melito of Sardis (9 to 11) compare the silent Isaac and the ram caught in the bush with Christ bound and crucified. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 4.5.4) says Abraham gave up his beloved son so that God might be pleased to give his own Son for Abraham's seed. Tertullian (Against the Jews 10) saw the wood Isaac carried as a figure of the cross, Origen preached his eighth homily on Genesis on the chapter, and Augustine (City of God 16.32) read the ram caught by its horns in thorns as Christ crowned with thorns.

The Qur'an tells the story briefly (37:99-111): Abraham sees in a dream that he is to sacrifice his son, the son tells him to do as he is commanded, and God ransoms him ‘with a great sacrifice’. Modern readings are treated in the hard questions: Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling (1843), Kant's objection in The Conflict of the Faculties (1798), Levenson (1993), Carol Delaney's Abraham on Trial (1998), Moberly's The Bible, Theology, and Faith (2000), and Omri Boehm's The Binding of Isaac (2007).

In art the binding is painted above the Torah niche of the synagogue at Dura-Europos (before AD 244), set in the sixth-century mosaic floor at Beth Alpha, and was the set subject of the 1401 competition for the Florence Baptistery doors, won by Lorenzo Ghiberti over Filippo Brunelleschi (both panels are in the Bargello). Caravaggio (about 1603, Uffizi) and Rembrandt (1635, Hermitage) painted the angel seizing Abraham's hand. Benjamin Britten set the Chester mystery play as Canticle II, Abraham and Isaac (1952); Wilfred Owen's ‘The Parable of the Old Man and the Young’ (published 1920) retold it as the slaughter of the First World War; and Stravinsky set the Hebrew text in Abraham and Isaac (1962-1963). The chapter is read at the Easter Vigil in Roman Catholic and many Protestant churches, on the Second Sunday of Lent in Year B of the Roman lectionary, and at Proper 8 in Year A of the Revised Common Lectionary, and the Roman Canon of the Mass names the sacrifice of ‘our father Abraham’.
text:
English Bibles differ at several points in this chapter.

In verse 1 the King James Version reads ‘God did tempt Abraham’; in 1611 ‘tempt’ could mean to try or prove, and modern versions read ‘tested’. In verse 2 the Septuagint renders ‘your only son’ as ‘your beloved son’ and the land of Moriah as ‘the high land’, the Latin Vulgate has ‘the land of vision’, linking the name to the verb see, and the Samaritan Pentateuch reads Moreh, the place near Shechem (12:6).

In verse 13 the Masoretic Text reads achar, ‘behind’, so ‘a ram behind him’ (KJV ‘behind him a ram’, BSB “behind him a ram”). Many Hebrew manuscripts, the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint, and the Syriac read echad, ‘one’ or ‘a’, and some modern versions (the NRSV, for example) follow them with ‘a ram’; in Hebrew the two words differ only by the similar letters d and r. In verse 14 the proverb can be read ‘on the mountain of the LORD it will be provided’ (BSB, NIV) or ‘he will be seen’ or ‘he will appear’; the Hebrew verb is the passive of the verb in the place name, and the play is probably deliberate.

In verse 17 ‘their enemies’ renders a Hebrew singular pronoun, literally ‘his enemies’, agreeing with the singular noun offspring; some interpreters see in the singular a hint of one individual descendant (see the verse note). In verse 18 the verb for ‘will be blessed’ is a Hithpael, which may also mean ‘will bless themselves’ (so the RSV); the Septuagint and the New Testament read the passive. The Hebrew and English verse numbers are the same throughout.

teach.big: God tests Abraham by asking for the son of promise, and Abraham's costly trust is met by God's provision of a substitute, so that the mountain of the test becomes the place where the LORD provides.

outline.t: God tests the faith he created, asking for the one gift that carries all his promises. The command names the love before it names the cost.
Abraham obeys at once and in silence, and tells the servants that ‘we’ will return: trust holds to God's promise even where it cannot see how.
Father and son walk together; Isaac asks the chapter's question, ‘where is the lamb?’, and Abraham answers better than he knows: God will provide.
At the last moment God stops the knife and provides a ram in Isaac's place. The God who tests is the God who provides, and the place is named for him, not for Abraham.
God swears by himself and renews every promise. The oath rests on God, and its reach is every nation of the earth.
Life goes on, and the story turns to the next generation: God is already preparing Rebekah, the wife through whom the promise will continue.

teach.pitfalls:
The most dangerous misreading turns the chapter into a model to imitate, as if God might ask any parent to harm a child and faith would mean obeying. The text itself stops the knife, and the rest of Scripture forbids child sacrifice absolutely (Deuteronomy 12:31, Jeremiah 7:31). The test was unique to Abraham's place in the story of the promise. A second misreading makes the point ‘give up whatever you love most to God’ and applies it lightly to a hobby or a habit. The chapter is about trusting God with the promise itself when his command seems to contradict it; it should not be trivialized.

A third pitfall ignores Isaac, turning him into a prop in his father's test, or ignores what the story cost. Tradition has asked what Isaac knew and felt, and the silence of verse 19, where he is not mentioned, invites that reflection without licensing speculation. A fourth pitfall reads every detail as a code for the cross, so that the donkey, the servants, and the knife each stand for something. The New Testament draws the main lines (the beloved and only son, God not sparing his Son, the resurrection figure, the Lamb); teach those clearly and mark later typology as the church's reflection. Finally, avoid presenting the chapter as a Christian possession only. It is central to Jewish prayer and Muslim devotion as well, and a teacher should be able to describe those readings fairly.
teach.pastoral: This text presses on parents, especially those who have lost a child, those watching a child suffer, and those who were harmed by a parent who claimed God's authority. Teach it with care. Say plainly that the chapter ends with the child spared and that God condemns harm to children; no one should hear from this text that God wants them to endure or inflict abuse. Those grieving a child may hear the story as a cruelty; let them know the Bible's own honesty about the weight of verse 2, and point them to the God who did not spare his own Son, and so knows the loss from inside. For people with scrupulous consciences who fear that God will demand whatever they love most, stress that the test was unique to Abraham and that its end is God's provision, not his cruelty. Keep a path to real help visible for anyone in danger at home.

hard.q: How could God command a father to sacrifice his son, and was Abraham right to obey?
hard.a:
This is one of the hardest chapters in the Bible, and the objection has been pressed by philosophers, Jewish scholars, and Christian readers alike. Immanuel Kant, in the first part of The Conflict of the Faculties (1798), argued that Abraham should have answered the voice that he was certain he ought not kill his good son, but could never be certain that the voice was God's; a command that contradicts the moral law cannot be recognized as divine. Carol Delaney (Abraham on Trial, 1998), an anthropologist, argued that the story has taught Judaism, Christianity, and Islam to honor a father's willingness to sacrifice his child and so has legitimated paternal power and obedience, and she proposed that it should no longer be held up as a model. Omri Boehm (The Binding of Isaac: A Religious Model of Disobedience, 2007), a Jewish philosopher, argued that the angel of verses 11 and 12 is a later addition and that in the earlier story Abraham chose on his own to sacrifice the ram instead of his son, an act of faithful disobedience; he claimed support from Maimonides and other medieval readers.

The responses are several. Søren Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling (1843), published under the pseudonym Johannes de silentio, accepted that Abraham's act cannot be justified by universal ethics; he called it a ‘teleological suspension of the ethical’ and presented Abraham as the ‘knight of faith’, whose trust in God cannot be explained in public terms, which is why the book insists on the terror of the story rather than softening it. Jewish tradition has often answered by attention to the text: the narrator tells the reader it is a test (verse 1), God stops it (verse 12), and the law and prophets reject child sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31). Jon Levenson (1993) rejected the modern idea that the story is only an etiology for replacing children with animals; he argued that it affirms God's real claim on the beloved son while showing that claim met by substitution and redemption, and that Abraham's greatness lies in his willingness to give God what was most precious. R. W. L. Moberly (The Bible, Theology, and Faith, 2000) read the story as defining the fear of God and showing Abraham's trust that God would provide, a trust confirmed at Moriah. Christian readers add Hebrews 11:19, which says Abraham expected God to keep his promise even through death, and the cross, where God did what he did not in the end require of Abraham. Critics reply that these readings explain Abraham's faith without removing the moral scandal of the command itself. Readers still differ on how to weigh the command against its outcome. The text does not ask anyone to make the difficulty disappear, and it has never been read in Jewish or Christian tradition as permission to harm a child.

hard.q: The Qur'an tells a similar story. Was the son Isaac or Ishmael?
hard.a:
The question arises because the Qur'an (37:99-111) tells of Abraham dreaming that he must sacrifice his son, of the son's willing consent, and of God ransoming him with a great sacrifice, but does not name the son, and only after the story (37:112) announces the birth of Isaac. Most Muslim commentators and the settled Muslim tradition hold that the son was Ishmael, the firstborn, and this is the event Muslims remember at Eid al-Adha. They point to the order of the Qur'an's narrative, in which Isaac's birth is announced after the sacrifice, and to Ishmael's association with Abraham at Mecca. Some critics of Genesis add that ‘your only son’ in verse 2 fits Ishmael poorly and Isaac only awkwardly, since Abraham had two sons.

Genesis itself names Isaac three times in the command and the narrative (verses 2, 3, and 9), and calls him ‘your only son’ in a sense the preceding chapter explains: Ishmael has been sent away (21:14), and God has said that Abraham's offspring will be reckoned through Isaac (21:12). Hebrews 11:17-18 and James 2:21 identify the son as Isaac. Within early Islamic scholarship itself opinion was divided: the commentator al-Tabari (died 923) records authorities on both sides and himself favored Isaac, and Ibn Ishaq also named Isaac, before the view that the son was Ishmael became dominant. Scholars of Qur'anic interpretation, such as Reuven Firestone (Journal of Semitic Studies, 1989), have traced how that consensus formed. Christians and Jews read Genesis as naming Isaac; Muslims read the Qur'an as meaning Ishmael. A fair teacher can state both, note that all three traditions honor Abraham's surrender to God, and let the texts speak for themselves.

observe: How does God describe Isaac in verse 2, and in what order do the descriptions come? Where are the same words repeated later in the chapter?
What does Abraham say to his servants in verse 5 and to Isaac in verse 8? What do the narrator and the angel say about the place in verses 13 and 14?
Who speaks in verses 15 to 18, what does he swear by, and what does he promise?
interpret: The narrator tells us in verse 1 that this is a test, but Abraham does not know it. How does that knowledge shape the way we read the rest of the chapter?
What is the relationship between Abraham's words in verse 8 and the name he gives the place in verse 14?
Hebrews 11:19 says Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead. How does that reading make sense of the tension between God's command and God's promise?
apply: Abraham was asked to trust God with the very thing God had promised him. What gift in your life is hardest to hold with an open hand, and why?
Isaac asked, ‘where is the lamb?’ How does the answer of this chapter, and of the cross, shape the way you think about God's provision?
The chapter leaves Abraham's and Isaac's feelings unspoken. How might you speak honestly to God about a command or a loss you do not understand?
